# 1. Introduction

Student mental health is a critical factor influencing academic performance, retention, and overall well-being in higher education.
Understanding which demographic, academic, social, and lifestyle variables correlate with student depression enables universities to identify at-risk individuals early and allocate targeted support resources effectively.

In this analysis, we examine the **Student Depression Dataset** (`4,464` student records across `13` features), which captures demographic attributes (`Gender`, `Age`, `Home_division`), socioeconomic and living conditions (`Family_background`, `Living_style`, `Cost_without_study`), academic standing (`Current_semester`, `CGPA`), and personal well-being indicators (`Relationship_status`, `Marital_status`, `friend_circle`, `Health_condition`). Our objective is to perform exploratory data analysis (EDA) to uncover key risk patterns and develop a supervised machine learning classification pipeline to predict whether a student experiences depression (`Depression`: `Yes` vs. `No`).

Data source: [Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mkhoirulmustaqim/student-depression-detection-dataset)


# 2. Data Loading & Initial Inspection

In this section, we load the student depression dataset and inspect the first few rows to understand the structure of the features and target variable (`Depression`).

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")

df = pd.read_csv('../data/Student_Depression_Dataset.csv')

print(df.head())
```

# 3. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

Before building any classification models, we inspect the dataset's dimensions, data types, missing values, and feature distributions. Understanding class balance and feature scales helps prevent data leakage and informs our preprocessing pipeline (such as scaling numerical features and encoding categorical variables).

```{python}
# Clean any leading/trailing whitespace in column names
df.columns = df.columns.str.strip()

print(f"Dataset Shape: {df.shape[0]} rows, {df.shape[1]} columns\n")
print("--- Data Types & Non-Null Counts ---")
df.info()

print("\n--- Missing Values ---")
missing = df.isnull().sum()
print(missing[missing > 0] if missing.sum() > 0 else "No missing values detected.")

print(f"\nDuplicate Rows: {df.duplicated().sum()}")
```

Next, we examine the distributions of our binary target variable, Depression, to check for class imbalance.

```{python}
import altair as alt

# Allow Altair to render datasets with >5,000 rows
alt.data_transformers.disable_max_rows()

# Clean any leading/trailing whitespace in column names
df.columns = df.columns.str.strip()

print(f"Dataset Shape: {df.shape[0]} rows, {df.shape[1]} columns\n")
print("--- Data Types & Non-Null Counts ---")
df.info()

print("\n--- Missing Values ---")
missing = df.isnull().sum()
print(missing[missing > 0] if missing.sum() > 0 else "No missing values detected.")

print(f"\nDuplicate Rows: {df.duplicated().sum()}")
```

```{python}
target_col = 'Depression'

bars = alt.Chart(df).mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X(f'{target_col}:N', title='Depression Status', axis=alt.Axis(labelAngle=0)),
    y=alt.Y('count():Q', title='Count'),
    color=alt.Color(f'{target_col}:N', legend=None, scale=alt.Scale(scheme='pastel1')),
    tooltip=[alt.Tooltip(f'{target_col}:N', title='Depression'), alt.Tooltip('count():Q', title='Count')]
).properties(
    width=300,
    height=250,
    title=f'Target Variable Distribution ({target_col})'
)

text = bars.mark_text(
    align='center',
    baseline='bottom',
    dy=-4
).encode(
    text='count():Q'
)

(bars + text)

```

Obviously the dataset we have is not balanced. We might need to class_weight="balanced" to combat this problem.

## Data Distribution of Numeric variables grouped by Target variable (Depression)

```{python}

num_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]).columns.tolist()

print(num_cols)


if num_cols:
    rows = []
    for col in num_cols:
        dens = alt.Chart(df).transform_density(
            col,
            as_=[col, 'density'],
            groupby=[target_col]
        ).mark_area(opacity=0.45).encode(
            x=alt.X(f'{col}:Q', title=col),
            y=alt.Y('density:Q', title='Density', stack=None),
            color=alt.Color(f'{target_col}:N', scale=alt.Scale(scheme='set2')),
            tooltip=[
                alt.Tooltip(f'{col}:Q', format='.2f'),
                alt.Tooltip('density:Q', format='.4f'),
                alt.Tooltip(f'{target_col}:N', title='Depression')
            ]
        ).properties(width=280, height=180, title=f'Normalized Density of {col}')

        box = alt.Chart(df).mark_boxplot(size=40).encode(
            x=alt.X(f'{target_col}:N', title='Depression', axis=alt.Axis(labelAngle=0)),
            y=alt.Y(f'{col}:Q', scale=alt.Scale(zero=False), title=col),
            color=alt.Color(f'{target_col}:N', scale=alt.Scale(scheme='set2'))
        ).properties(width=220, height=180, title=f'{col} by {target_col}')

        rows.append(alt.hconcat(dens, box))

alt.vconcat(*rows).resolve_scale(color='shared')

```

## Data Distribution of Categorical variables grouped by Target variable (Depression)


```{python}


cat_cols = [c for c in df.select_dtypes(include=['object', 'category']).columns if c != 'Depression']
overall_rate = (df['Depression'] == 'Yes').mean()

charts = []
for col in cat_cols:
    bars = alt.Chart(df).mark_bar(height=22).encode(
        y=alt.Y(f'{col}:N', title=None, sort='-x'),
        x=alt.X('count():Q', stack='normalize', axis=alt.Axis(format='%', title='Percentage (%)')),
        color=alt.Color('Depression:N', scale=alt.Scale(domain=['Yes', 'No'], range=['#fc8d62', '#66c2a5'])),
        order=alt.Order('Depression:N', sort='descending'),
        tooltip=[col, 'Depression', 'count()']
    )
    rule = alt.Chart(pd.DataFrame({'r': [overall_rate]})).mark_rule(strokeDash=[4, 4], size=1.5).encode(x='r:Q')
    
    charts.append((bars + rule).properties(width=260, height=alt.Step(30), title=col.replace('_', ' ')))

rows = [alt.hconcat(*charts[i:i+2], spacing=50) for i in range(0, len(charts), 2)]
alt.vconcat(*rows, spacing=30).resolve_scale(color='shared')
```
